title: Toldot: Rebekah asks why (Genesis 25:22)
hook: pregnant with struggling twins, she goes to inquire of the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac and Ishmael, long apart, burying their father together. Your line was brothers at the grave. Today, a new portion.

Three in the morning, and one question goes around and around. Why is this happening to me? Not the polite version. The real one. Isaac and Rebekah have been married twenty years, and there are no children. Isaac prays for his wife, and the prayer is answered. Then the pregnancy everyone wanted turns into something that frightens her. This week's portion is called Toldot, generations. Today: Rebekah asks why.
screen: `THE 3 A.M. QUESTION.` → `TWENTY YEARS OF WAITING.` → `TOLDOT: GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: Isaac is forty when he marries Rebekah, and sixty when their sons are born. Twenty years. The Torah says Isaac prayed opposite his wife, and the rabbis pictured them praying together, facing each other, each on behalf of the other. Then she conceives. Twins. And the children struggled together within her. The Hebrew verb is rough; Rashi hears in it both running and crushing. This isn't the glow of a happy pregnancy. It hurts, and it scares her. So Rebekah says something older English Bibles render, if it be so, why am I thus? The Hebrew is even shorter. Lamah zeh anochi. Why this, I? It's almost a broken sentence. Some translators hear, why is this happening to me? Others hear something darker. The old Jewish Publication Society translation has her say: "If it be so, wherefore do I live?" Nobody can be completely sure, and the broken grammar fits how pain talks. Then she doesn't only complain. She goes to inquire of the LORD. The Hebrew is lidrosh, to seek, the same root as midrash, the tradition of asking questions of the text. Rashi says she went to the house of study of Shem, Noah's son; the Torah doesn't say where. It only says she went, with her hardest question, and asked it out loud. Not Isaac, not a servant: Rebekah herself. And she's answered, as you'll hear tomorrow. The text doesn't tell her to hide her fear, or to be grateful and quiet. Her why is written into the Torah, and read aloud in synagogues every year.
screen: `TWENTY YEARS, THEN TWINS.` · `THE CHILDREN STRUGGLED WITHIN HER.` · `LAMAH ZEH ANOCHI: WHY THIS, I?` · `SHE WENT TO INQUIRE.` · then, large: `WHY AM I THUS?`

segments.voice: Let one real why come up: why this illness, why this loss, why me, why now, as blunt as Rebekah's, not tidied into something polite. If you pray, you can bring it to God in exactly those words. If you don't, simply hold it, and notice that asking is already a kind of seeking.
Toldot. Generations: the portion of Isaac and Rebekah's family, which opens with twenty years of waiting and one blunt question.
Your line: why am I thus. Rebekah asked it out loud, and went to seek. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish prayer, from the Psalms to personal prayer, makes room for complaint and hard questions, and Jews often bring their questions to a rabbi or a study partner as a form of seeking.

sources.quoted: If it be so, wherefore do I live?

notes: The carry 'why am I thus' follows the KJV of Genesis 25:22, so the quotation is cited to the KJV rather than JPS 1917 (whose wording, possibly 'wherefore do I live?', was not verified). A Keeper may prefer the JPS wording.
Isaac praying 'opposite his wife' (le-nochach ishto) and the image of the two praying facing each other: Rashi on 25:21; confirm.
Rashi on 25:22 (she went to the study house of Shem): given without naming Shem; confirm.
Ages 40 and 60 from Genesis 25:20 and 25:26; confirm.
